payload.rationale: The event requires NASA GISS's 2026 LOTI anomaly to exceed both the 2025 value and 1.28°C, i.e., effectively to beat the 2024 record (reported at ~1.28°C, so at least 1.29°C is needed after rounding). Background: 2025 was widely reported as the second- or third-warmest year, roughly 1.20–1.26°C on the GISS scale, below 2024. Late-2025 forecasts (Met Office, Berkeley Earth-style outlooks) placed 2026 most likely in the top three but slightly below the 2024 record, given weak La Niña/neutral ENSO conditions entering 2026. A record in 2026 would most plausibly require a rapid El Niño onset by mid-2026 plus continued strong background warming; even then, El Niño's largest imprint on the global annual mean usually falls in the following year. Given the long-term trend (~0.2–0.25°C/decade) and the possibility of a fast-developing El Niño, a record is plausible but less likely than not. Too high: if ENSO stayed neutral or cool through 2026 and aerosol/solar contributions faded, 2026 would likely land near 1.20–1.26°C, clearly missing the threshold; ties at 1.28 also fail. Too low: 2023–2025 warmth persistently exceeded model expectations, and if El Niño emerged strongly by mid-2026 with an anomalously warm first half, 2026 could plausibly reach 1.30°C+, as some outlooks allowed. Without observed 2026 monthly GISS data (which would exist as of the Sept 2026 cutoff but were not supplied), I rely on pre-year outlooks and settle near 0.3.
limitations: No supplied evidence; no access to 2026 monthly GISS anomalies or ENSO state as of the information cutoff.
Exact GISS 2025 annual value and any dataset revisions unknown.
Resolution depends on rounding of GISS reported values; a tie at 1.28°C resolves No.
Estimate relies on general recollection of late-2025 outlooks, which may be imprecise.
